stall.lastCandidateQuestion:
Beyond pricing, a few levers. One, procurement — renegotiate or consolidate vendors, lock in longer contracts or hedge beans, explore private label on packaging and food. Two, waste reduction, since spoilage on dairy and food runs straight through COGS. Three, mix shift — push higher-margin items like brewed coffee and retail beans over milk-heavy drinks. Four, portion and recipe standardization. Five, overhead, which crept 12 to 14 points and is worth $9.6M on $480M.

But pricing is the big one. On $480M, a 5% price increase is $24M of near-pure margin, roughly 5 points.

Could I get: one, current COGS dollars. Two, overhead breakdown. Three, waste rate. Four, item-level margins. Five, supplier contract lengths. Six, brand premium data. Seven, peer margin benchmarks. Eight, any pilot test capability?

turns.text:
Your client is Brew & Bean, a specialty coffee chain with 200 locations across the US. Over the past two years, their net profit margin has declined from 24% to 6%, even though revenues have grown 15% over the same period. The CEO has hired us to identify the root cause of this profit decline and recommend how to reverse it. How would you approach this problem?

Take a moment, then walk me through how you'd approach this.

Okay, so profit is revenue minus costs, and revenue is up while margin is down, which points at costs. Before I structure it, could I get a few data points?

One, the full cost breakdown by line item for both years. Two, COGS as a percent of revenue. Three, labor costs per store. Four, rent and occupancy costs. Five, the number of stores two years ago versus today. Six, average customer wait time. Seven, employee turnover rate. Eight, the mix of revenue between drinks, food, and retail beans.

That would let me see where the eighteen points of margin went.

Before I give you any data, I want to see how you'd organize the problem. I don't have average customer wait time, employee turnover rate or the revenue mix between drinks, food, and retail beans. I'll come back to the full cost breakdown by line item for both years, COGS as a percent of revenue, labor costs per store, rent and occupancy costs and the number of stores two years ago versus today shortly. Take a minute if you need it, then walk me through your structure for finding the root cause.

Sure. At a high level I'd split profit into revenue and costs. On revenue, volume times price — store count, transactions per store, average ticket. On costs, fixed versus variable: COGS, labor, rent, marketing, corporate overhead, and then any one-time items like new store buildouts or impairments.

To actually drive that, could I get a few more things? One, average ticket size by year. Two, transactions per store per day. Three, coffee bean commodity prices over the two years. Four, menu price changes by year. Five, wage rates per hour by market. Six, marketing spend.七 — sorry, seven, same-store sales growth. Eight, capex on new store openings.

Those would let me pin down which line moved.

Okay. I don't have transactions per store per day, wage rates per hour by market, marketing spend, same-store sales growth or capex on new store openings. I'll come back to average ticket size by year, coffee bean commodity prices over the two years and menu price changes by year shortly. Looking at that structure as a whole, is it MECE, and which branch would you prioritize first, and why?

I think it's broadly MECE — revenue and cost don't overlap, and within cost I've split fixed and variable. There may be a little overlap between corporate overhead and marketing, so I'd fold marketing under overhead.

On where to start, I'd rather let the data point me there than guess. Could I get a few more items? One, gross margin by year. Two, EBITDA by year. Three, store-level P&L for a typical location. Four, number of employees per store. Five, delivery and third-party app fees. Six, packaging and cup costs. Seven, utilities per store. Eight, any franchise versus company-owned split.

And separately, if it exists, a split of the single largest cost line into its components — that's probably where the eighteen points sit.

Okay. You asked about this earlier: COGS is 58% of revenue today, up from 42% two years ago. Labor is 22% of revenue, and it’s been stable. Overhead is 14% of revenue, up slightly from 12%. I don't have gross margin by year, EBITDA by year, a store-level P&L for a typical location, number of employees per store, delivery and third-party app fees, packaging and cup costs, utilities per store or a franchise versus company-owned split. I'll come back to the number of stores two years ago versus today and a split of the single largest cost line into its components shortly. You said you'd let the data point you rather than guess. Given what you know about the client so far, which branch is your starting hypothesis, and what would you expect that data to show?

COGS is the branch — it moved 16 points of the 18, and labor is flat, so that's where it is. My hypothesis is input costs rose, most likely green coffee beans or dairy, and menu prices didn't move with them.

To confirm, could I get: one, the COGS split into beans, dairy, food, and packaging. Two, bean cost per pound by year. Three, dairy cost per gallon by year. Four, waste and spoilage rate. Five, supplier contract terms and whether any hedges rolled off. Six, menu price changes by year. Seven, average ticket by year. Eight, units sold by year.

If beans and dairy are most of COGS and prices held flat, that's the answer.

Okay. Coming back to what you asked for earlier: Coffee beans were 25% of COGS two years ago. Other input costs — dairy, packaging, and food — are up 37.5% over the past two years. Raw coffee bean costs are up 40% over the past two years. I don't have waste and spoilage rate, supplier contract terms and hedges or units sold by year. I'll come back to menu price changes by year, average ticket by year and the number of stores two years ago versus today shortly. You said COGS moved 16 of the 18 points. Walk me through how you got that, and what base those points are measured against.

Both are measured as a percent of revenue, so they're directly comparable. COGS went from 42% to 58% of revenue, that's 16 points. Overhead went 12% to 14%, 2 points. Labor flat at 22%. So 16 plus 2 equals 18, which exactly matches the margin drop from 24% to 6%. The pieces reconcile, so nothing's hiding elsewhere.

Could I also get: one, menu price changes by year. Two, average ticket by year. Three, beans as a percent of COGS today versus the 25% two years ago. Four, dairy as a share of COGS. Five, revenue in absolute dollars for both years. Six, store count both years. Seven, cost per cup. Eight, whether they tried any price increases and how customers responded.

Okay. On what you asked about earlier: Menu prices have not changed in two years. The average transaction is $6.80, up from $6.20 two years ago — about a 10% increase, because customers are buying more items per visit. 200 stores today — and it was 200 stores two years ago, so the footprint hasn’t changed. Take a look at this: Brew & Bean Cost Structure Over Time. I don't have beans as a percent of COGS today, dairy as a share of COGS, cost per cup or price increase attempts and customer response. I'll come back to revenue in absolute dollars for both years shortly. Take a look at this exhibit. What does it tell you about where the COGS increase is coming from?

The exhibit shows it's a steady climb, 42 to 50 to 58, about 8 points a year, not a one-time shock. So it's ongoing input inflation, not a single bad contract.

And the math says it isn't just coffee. Beans were 25% of COGS and rose 40%; the other 75% rose 37.5%. Weighted: 0.25 × 40% + 0.75 × 37.5% = 10% + 28.1% = 38.1% overall COGS inflation. So it's broad-based across beans, dairy, packaging, food — beans aren't the villain, they're a quarter of it. And with menu prices flat for two years, none of that got passed through.

Could I get: one, revenue in absolute dollars both years. Two, competitor pricing. Three, price elasticity estimates. Four, customer loyalty data. Five, regional cost variation. Six, 2024 bean futures. Seven, vendor concentration. Eight, any private-label options.

Okay. You asked about this earlier: Total revenue is $480M a year. I don't have competitor pricing, price elasticity estimates, customer loyalty data, regional cost variation, 2024 bean futures, vendor concentration or private-label options. You say the 38.1% overall input inflation went unpassed because menu prices are flat, yet COGS rose from 42% to 58% of revenue. Walk me through how those two figures fit together, given that revenue per transaction rose.

They fit almost exactly. Take 42% × 1.381 = 58.0%. That's the observed number. So the entire COGS increase is explained by input inflation with zero price pass-through — nothing else is needed.

And the ticket increase doesn't help, because it came from customers buying more items, not paying more per item. More items means proportionally more cost, so revenue and COGS scale together and the ratio stays put. A $6.20 to $6.80 ticket from volume is margin-neutral; only a price increase would have moved the percentage.

Could I get: one, items per transaction both years. Two, transaction count. Three, revenue two years ago. Four, gross profit dollars. Five, store-level breakeven. Six, discount and promo spend. Seven, loyalty program economics. Eight, any menu engineering data.

Okay. I don't have items per transaction both years, transaction count, revenue two years ago, gross profit dollars, store-level breakeven, discount and promo spend, loyalty program economics or menu engineering data. Beyond what we've discussed so far, what else could Brew & Bean do to reverse this margin decline?

Beyond pricing, a few levers. One, procurement — renegotiate or consolidate vendors, lock in longer contracts or hedge beans, explore private label on packaging and food. Two, waste reduction, since spoilage on dairy and food runs straight through COGS. Three, mix shift — push higher-margin items like brewed coffee and retail beans over milk-heavy drinks. Four, portion and recipe standardization. Five, overhead, which crept 12 to 14 points and is worth $9.6M on $480M.

But pricing is the big one. On $480M, a 5% price increase is $24M of near-pure margin, roughly 5 points.

Could I get: one, current COGS dollars. Two, overhead breakdown. Three, waste rate. Four, item-level margins. Five, supplier contract lengths. Six, brand premium data. Seven, peer margin benchmarks. Eight, any pilot test capability?

Okay. I don't have current COGS dollars, overhead breakdown, waste rate, item-level margins, supplier contract lengths, brand premium data, peer margin benchmarks or pilot test capability. You said overhead is worth $9.6M on $480M. Walk me through that.

Sorry, I was loose there. Overhead at 14% of $480M is $67.2M total. What I meant is the increase: overhead went from 12% to 14%, so 2 points on $480M is $9.6M of annual profit that's leaked out since two years ago. That's the recoverable piece, not the whole line.

For scale, COGS at 58% is $278.4M, and had it stayed at 42% it'd be $201.6M — so roughly $77M of the gap sits there. That's where the real money is, and it dwarfs overhead.

Could I get: one, what's inside overhead — corporate versus store-level. Two, headcount at corporate. Three, tech or systems spend. Four, any new initiatives launched in the last two years. Five, G&A per store. Six, rent escalators. Seven, insurance costs. Eight, D&A.

Okay. I don't have what's inside overhead, corporate headcount, tech or systems spend, new initiatives launched in the last two years, G&A per store, rent escalators, insurance costs or D&A. The CEO walks in and asks for your recommendation in a couple of minutes. What do you tell them?

My recommendation is to raise menu prices — that's the root cause and the fastest fix.

Here's the logic. Margin fell 18 points, from 24% to 6%. COGS accounts for 16 of those, rising 42% to 58% of revenue. Input costs rose 38% across the board — beans up 40%, everything else up 37.5% — and 42% × 1.381 gets you to 58%, so inflation explains the decline entirely. Meanwhile menu prices haven't moved in two years. Ticket is up from $6.20 to $6.80, but that's more items per visit, which is margin-neutral.

So: a 5% price increase on $480M is roughly $24M, about 5 margin points. Pair it with procurement renegotiation and the 2-point overhead creep, worth $9.6M.

Risks: elasticity is unknown and volume could drop, so I'd pilot across a subset of stores first and measure transaction counts before rolling national.

Okay. The COGS gap you sized earlier is closer to 76.8, not 9.6 for the overhead piece, so let's take that figure and keep going: the overhead creep is worth 9.6M, and the COGS gap is 76.8M. You named elasticity as a risk and proposed a pilot. What is the biggest risk to your recommendation, and how would you decide from the pilot results whether to roll it out?

Biggest risk is that a 5% price increase drives more than 5% volume loss — specialty coffee is discretionary and there's cheap competition. And because COGS is 58% of revenue, I only keep about 42 cents of each lost dollar, so the breakeven on volume decline is roughly 5% ÷ ... actually it's contribution-based: I'd lose 42% margin on departing transactions and gain 5 points on the rest. Rough breakeven is around 10% volume loss, so I'd have real room.

Decision rule from the pilot: run 20 stores, 8–12 weeks, matched control stores. Roll out if transaction counts fall under that breakeven and gross profit dollars per store rise. Watch repeat visit frequency, not just one-week shock.

Could I get: one, historical response to any prior price move. Two, competitor price points. Three, transaction counts by store. Four, regional demographics.
Average revenue per store is $2.4M a year. I don't have Competitor price points or Regional demographics. That's time. Thanks for working through it — your written report will follow.

modelAnswerJsonb.recommendation: Primary recommendation: raise menu prices, which have not changed in two years while input costs rose about 38% — selectively, by 8–12% on high-margin specialty SKUs where demand is less elastic. Pair it with procurement across all inputs, not just beans: multi-year bean supply contracts plus renegotiated dairy and packaging supply, since beans explain only about a quarter of the COGS increase. Secondary: pilot a lower-cost 'commodity blend' for budget-conscious locations. Do not recommend blanket cost cuts — labor and overhead are already lean.
